Anti-government protesters gather in front of Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi airport early Wednesday. The newly married husband and wife, in Thailand for their  honeymoon, were struggling to find a way home to California after explosions at two Bangkok airports wounded four people and both  airports were shut down. The People's Alliance for Democracy , which is leading the protests, said it will not end its occupation of the airports until the prime minister resigns. They accuse his government of being a front for ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. Ongoing protests caused authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport, which handles 60,000 incoming passengers daily, an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond told CNN. Pro- and anti-government protesters also exchanged gunfire Tuesday, a Thai police official said. Protesters with golf clubs and long wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with each side throwing objects at the other.  Watch what's causing the protests » . Protesters blockaded people trying to get to one of the airports. They directed travelers to exit onto the access roads.  See more photos » . "I'm trying to get out of this place, but I'm stuck," iReporter Arjan Sing, who was on a two-week vacation to India and stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend's family. "When we took the exit there were lots of tourists standing around wondering what they were going to do." Gannon said the situation started off fairly relaxed, but tensions were escalating. "As more and more tourists leave [the airport], the fact that we don't have any information and there's no one to give us information, now we feel stranded here and we don't know where to go," Gannon said. "It seems a little bit more hostile than it was earlier." Gannon said she's heard nothing from airport personnel and her quest for answers is hurt even more by the fact that many people in the airport speak no English. "I don't know what happened to my flight," one woman waiting in an airport told CNN. "They won't talk to us and I'm angry and sad because I have two small children and they're sick so we want to go home." The airlines have also been mum on the situation, Gannon said, making it difficult for them to decide whether to wait it out at the airport or try to find a hotel. "We've had absolutely no contact from our air carrier," Gannon said. "But that seems to be universal across the board." One traveler said the wait was frustrating. "They've started coming through and telling us that we possibly might be out of here in the morning," he told CNN. "But either way, there's no problem. We just sit here and relax and enjoy the ride." Gannon said she and her new spouse just hope to get home sometime in the near future. "We've been gone for 17 days and [the honeymoon] was good -- until now," she said. "We are just trying to go home, get back to work and Thanksgiving."

outputs.L1:
**BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN)** -- For 17 hours, Kerri Gannon and her husband remained stranded at a Bangkok airport on Wednesday, searching for a way home to the United States after the facility was overrun by protesters and forced to close. Anti-government demonstrators gathered outside Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport early that morning, compounding the couple's difficulties.

The newlyweds, who had traveled to Thailand for their honeymoon, found themselves struggling to arrange passage back to California after explosions at two Bangkok airports left four people injured and prompted the closure of both facilities. The previous day, thousands of anti-government protesters had stormed the airports in opposition to the return of Thai Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat from an economic summit in Peru.

"The upper level outside is really crowded with protesters, and for the most part they're kind of quiet and polite," Gannon said, speaking from the airport. "They're roaming the airport, cheering, clapping, and walking around—but it's clearly their domain."

*Watch protesters clash »*

It remained unclear which of the two occupied airports she was calling from, though tourists were stranded at both locations. The People's Alliance for Democracy, the group leading the protests, has stated it will not end its occupation until the prime minister resigns, accusing his government of serving as a proxy for ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

The ongoing unrest forced authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport—which typically handles 60,000 arriving passengers daily—according to an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond who spoke with CNN. A Thai police official also reported that pro- and anti-government protesters exchanged gunfire on Tuesday, while demonstrators armed with golf clubs and wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with both sides hurling objects at one another.

*Watch what's causing the protests »*

Protesters blockaded routes to one of the airports, redirecting travelers toward the access roads instead.

*See more photos »*

"I'm trying to get out of this place, but I'm stuck," said iReporter Arjan Singh, who had been on a two-week vacation to India and stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend's family. "When we took the exit, there were lots of tourists standing around, wondering what they were going to do."

Gannon noted that while the situation initially seemed relatively calm, tensions had begun to escalate. "As more and more tourists leave the airport, and given that we have no information and no one to provide it, we now feel stranded here with nowhere to go," she said. "It seems a bit more hostile than it did earlier."

Gannon reported receiving no communication from airport personnel, a challenge made worse by the fact that many people at the airport did not speak English. "I don't know what happened to my flight," one woman waiting at the airport told CNN. "They won't talk to us, and I'm angry and sad because I have two small children who are sick, and we just want to go home."

According to Gannon, the airlines have likewise remained silent on the matter, complicating travelers' decisions about whether to wait out the situation at the airport or seek lodging at a hotel. "We've had absolutely no contact from our air carrier," she said, "but that seems to be the case across the board."

One traveler expressed frustration with the prolonged wait. "They've started coming through and telling us that we might possibly be out of here by morning," he told CNN. "But either way, there's no problem—we'll just sit here, relax, and see how it goes."

For her part, Gannon said she and her new husband simply hope to return home in the near future. "We've been gone for 17 days, and the honeymoon was wonderful—until now," she said. "We're just trying to get home, get back to work, and celebrate Thanksgiving."

# Stranded in Bangkok: Honeymooners Caught in Political Chaos

Kerri Gannon and her newlywed husband had hoped to end their honeymoon with a smooth journey home to California. Instead, they found themselves stranded for 17 grueling hours at Bangkok's airport, desperately searching for any possible way to return home as the airport around them descended into political turmoil.

The couple's ordeal began when anti-government protesters stormed and occupied Bangkok's two main airports, a dramatic escalation that forced aviation authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights. The sudden shutdown left thousands of tourists in the same predicament as the Gannons—stranded with no clear timeline for when they might be able to leave the country.

The situation grew increasingly volatile as the standoff continued. Explosions rocked the airport complex, wounding four people caught in the chaos. Beyond the blasts, violence erupted in other forms as well: protesters and taxi drivers clashed physically, wielding golf clubs and wooden sticks against one another in scattered skirmishes. Adding to the danger, gunfire was exchanged between pro-government and anti-government factions, transforming what should have been a bustling international travel hub into a scene of genuine unrest.

At the center of the occupation was the People's Alliance for Democracy, the group spearheading the protests. Its leaders made their demands clear and non-negotiable: they vowed to continue occupying the airports until Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat stepped down from power. The Alliance accused Wongsawat's government of serving merely as a puppet regime—a front designed to protect the interests of ousted former leader Thaksin Shinawatra, whose political influence they claimed still loomed large behind the scenes.

Yet amid this backdrop of explosions, street violence, and political brinkmanship, Gannon's firsthand account offered a somewhat different perspective on the atmosphere inside the terminal itself. She described the protesters who had taken over the airport as surprisingly quiet and polite in their demeanor. There was no sense of the protesters being hostile or aggressive toward stranded travelers like herself. Nevertheless, despite their calm behavior, it was unmistakably clear to Gannon that these protesters held firm control over the facility, dictating the terms of an occupation that showed no signs of ending soon and leaving travelers like her and her husband with little choice but to wait it out.

BANGKOK, Thailand — Kerri Gannon had imagined her honeymoon ending with a relaxing flight home, not with armed guards, explosions in the distance, and a night spent sleeping on the floor of a terminal surrounded by thousands of other stranded travelers. Instead, she and her husband found themselves among the estimated tens of thousands of passengers trapped inside Bangkok's two major airports after anti-government protesters stormed the facilities in a dramatic escalation of Thailand's prolonged political crisis.

"We just got married, and this is definitely not how we pictured spending the first days after our wedding," Gannon said, sitting amid piles of luggage and exhausted travelers at Suvarnabhumi International Airport. "There are people sleeping everywhere, families with young children, elderly travelers who don't know what to do. Nobody really knows how long this is going to last."

The chaos began when members of the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), a protest group that has been leading demonstrations against the government for months, broke through security barriers and occupied the grounds of Suvarnabhumi, one of Asia's busiest air travel hubs, as well as the older Don Mueang Airport, which has been used for domestic and some charter flights. The protesters are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat, whom they accuse of being a proxy for his brother-in-law, former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in a military coup in 2006 and now lives in self-imposed exile to avoid a corruption conviction.

The occupation quickly turned volatile. Witnesses reported hearing explosions and gunfire near the airport perimeter, and clashes broke out between protesters and taxi drivers who depend on the airport for their livelihoods and were angered by the disruption to their business. Video footage circulating in local media showed scuffles, overturned barricades, and security personnel struggling to maintain order as the situation spiraled out of control.

Airport authorities, faced with an increasingly dangerous and unmanageable situation, made the unprecedented decision to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at Suvarnabhumi, an airport that under normal circumstances handles approximately 60,000 passengers a day and serves as a critical gateway for both tourists and business travelers throughout Southeast Asia. The shutdown left airlines scrambling to reroute flights to other countries, including Malaysia and Singapore, while thousands of passengers already in transit found themselves stuck with nowhere to go.

Inside the terminals, the scene grew increasingly chaotic as the hours wore on. Airport staff struggled to provide food, water, and basic accommodations for the swelling crowd of stranded passengers. Some travelers described improvising sleeping arrangements using blankets from duty-free shops, while others attempted to charter buses or trains to neighboring countries in hopes of catching flights from alternate airports.

"It's honestly like nothing I've ever experienced," said one Australian backpacker who had been due to catch a connecting flight home. "One minute everything seemed normal, and the next there were guards everywhere, and everyone was being told the airport was closed indefinitely."

The airport occupation represents one of the most severe escalations yet in a political standoff that has gripped Thailand for months, pitting supporters of Prime Minister Somchai's government against the PAD, whose members argue that Thaksin's allies continue to exert improper influence over the country's politics through elected proxies. The demonstrators have previously stormed government buildings, including a lengthy occupation of Government House, the prime minister's official offices, but the seizure of the country's main international airport marks a significant and alarming shift in tactics.

Analysts warn that the disruption could have severe economic consequences for Thailand, a country heavily dependent on tourism and international trade. With flights canceled indefinitely and foreign governments beginning to issue travel warnings, the economic toll of the airport closures is expected to mount quickly, compounding the political uncertainty already weighing on the country.

For travelers like Gannon and her husband, however, the immediate concern was far more personal than the broader political implications. "We just want to get home," she said. "This was supposed to be one of the best trips of our lives, and now we're just trying to figure out how to get out of here safely."

As night fell over Bangkok, with the sound of intermittent explosions still echoing in the distance and thousands of passengers bedding down for another uncertain night inside the terminal, there was no clear indication of when—or how—the standoff might be resolved.

# Bangkok: Thailand's Vibrant Capital

Bangkok, the capital city of Thailand, stands as one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic metropolitan centers. This bustling city seamlessly blends ancient traditions with modern urban life, making it a fascinating subject for international media coverage.

CNN has frequently featured Bangkok in its reporting, covering topics ranging from political developments and economic trends to cultural events and tourism. As Thailand's political, economic, and cultural hub, Bangkok regularly draws the attention of international news organizations seeking to understand broader regional dynamics in Southeast Asia.

The city itself offers a striking contrast of experiences. Towering skyscrapers rise alongside golden Buddhist temples, while traditional floating markets operate not far from ultra-modern shopping malls. The Chao Phraya River, which winds through the city, has historically served as a vital artery for trade and transportation, and remains central to Bangkok's identity today.

Thailand's tourism industry, heavily centered on Bangkok as an entry point, contributes significantly to the national economy. International visitors are drawn to the city's street food culture, ornate temples like Wat Arun and Wat Phra Kaew, and vibrant nightlife districts. CNN's travel segments have often highlighted these attractions, introducing global audiences to Bangkok's unique character.

Beyond tourism, Bangkok serves as a critical hub for business and diplomacy in the region. Many multinational corporations maintain regional headquarters there, and the city hosts numerous international conferences and diplomatic meetings, further cementing its importance on the global stage.

As Thailand continues to navigate various political and economic challenges, Bangkok remains at the center of these developments, ensuring that international news outlets like CNN continue to monitor and report on this ever-evolving city.

**Thousands of Tourists Stranded as Protesters Shut Down Bangkok Airports**

*By CNN Staff*

BANGKOK, Thailand — Thousands of travelers, including hundreds of Americans, remained stranded Wednesday as anti-government protesters continued their occupation of Bangkok's two main airports, paralyzing air travel in and out of the Thai capital.

Suvarnabhumi Airport, one of Southeast Asia's busiest aviation hubs, has been shut down since Tuesday after members of the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD) stormed the terminal, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat. Don Mueang Airport, which handles domestic and some charter flights, was also forced to close as protesters expanded their demonstration.

The closures have left an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 travelers stuck inside the terminals, with thousands more unable to reach the airport or rebook flights out of the country. Airlines have canceled all incoming and outgoing flights indefinitely, and it remains unclear when normal operations might resume.

For American tourists caught in the chaos, the experience has ranged from frustrating to frightening.

"We've been sleeping on the floor for two nights now," said Karen Whitfield, a schoolteacher from Sacramento, California, who was traveling with her husband on what was supposed to be the final leg of a two-week vacation. "There's no information, nobody really knows what's happening next. We just keep hearing rumors."

Other travelers described scenes of confusion as protesters, many wearing the yellow shirts associated with the royalist PAD movement, filled the terminals with tents, sound systems, and makeshift barricades.

"It was surreal," said Mark Delgado, a businessman from Chicago who had arrived at Suvarnabhumi just as the protests intensified. "One minute we're going through customs, the next there are thousands of people setting up camp in the check-in area. Security just kind of stepped back and let it happen."

The U.S. Embassy in Bangkok issued a statement urging American citizens to avoid the airport entirely and to monitor local news for updates, while acknowledging the difficulty many faced in finding alternate routes home.

"We understand the concern and frustration among U.S. citizens affected by this situation," the embassy said. "We are working to provide updated information as it becomes available and encourage travelers to remain patient and seek alternative accommodations if possible."

With no clear timeline for reopening, some travelers have opted to make the long journey overland to airports in other cities, including Phuket and Chiang Mai, in hopes of catching flights out of the country. Others have simply hunkered down, waiting for a resolution to the political standoff that has gripped Thailand for months.

"At this point, we just want to get home," Whitfield said. "But we also understand this isn't about us. This is their country, their political crisis. We're just caught in the middle of it."

The protests are the latest escalation in a monthslong standoff between the PAD and the Thai government, part of a broader political crisis that has deeply divided the country since the ousting of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra in a 2006 military coup.

Thai officials have not indicated when the airports might reopen, and the government has faced criticism both domestically and internationally for its handling of the crisis.

CNN will continue to update this story as more information becomes available.

# Bangkok Airport Shutdown Strands Thousands, Including Newlyweds Desperate to Get Home

**BANGKOK** — What was meant to be the final chapter of a dream honeymoon turned into a days-long ordeal for one couple among thousands of travelers stranded when anti-government protesters stormed and occupied Suvarnabhumi Airport, forcing the closure of Thailand's main international gateway.

The airport, usually bustling with over 100,000 passengers daily, fell eerily silent this week as demonstrators from the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD) set up camp in the terminals, part of an escalating campaign to unseat the Thai government. Camping mats, makeshift barricades, and protest banners replaced check-in queues, while thousands of foreign tourists found themselves trapped in a country they could no longer easily leave.

Among them were newlyweds who had arrived in Thailand weeks earlier for what they described as "the trip of a lifetime" — pristine beaches, temple visits, and quiet evenings watching the sunset over the Andaman Sea.

"We had our flight booked, bags packed, everything ready to go home," said the husband, still in visible disbelief as he described the scene at the airport. "Then we get there and there's this sea of people, tents everywhere, and someone tells us the airport is closed indefinitely. Closed. Like, not delayed — closed."

The couple said they first heard rumblings of the protests through hotel staff and other travelers but had no idea the situation would escalate to a full takeover of the airport.

"We kept thinking, surely this will resolve itself in a day or two," the wife said. "But then a day became three days, and three days became not knowing when we'd see home again."

With commercial flights grounded and the airport's status uncertain, the pair — like thousands of others — were forced to scramble for alternative accommodation, extend hotel stays they hadn't budgeted for, and constantly refresh news sites and embassy advisories for any sign of resolution.

"Money was becoming a real issue," the husband admitted. "We'd planned this trip down to the last day. Suddenly we're paying for extra nights, extra meals, and just... waiting."

Foreign embassies, including those of the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, issued urgent travel advisories, with some governments arranging alternate departure points via airports in Phuket or Chiang Mai, or even coordinating bus transfers to neighboring countries where travelers could catch outbound flights.

The couple said they spent hours calling their airline and embassy, often met with busy signals or vague assurances.

"At one point we considered just taking a bus to Cambodia and flying out from Phnom Penh," the wife said. "We were ready to do anything at that point. We just wanted to get home."

Thai authorities, caught in a tense standoff with protest leaders, offered little clarity in the early days of the occupation, further fueling anxiety among stranded travelers. The economic toll on Thailand's vital tourism sector mounted by the hour, with airlines cancelling flights en masse and tour operators scrambling to reroute clients.

For the honeymooners, the ordeal became an unwanted extension of their trip — one filled not with romance, but uncertainty.

"It's almost funny, looking back," the husband said with a tired laugh. "We came here to celebrate starting our life together, and instead we got a crash course in patience and Thai politics."

As of this report, the couple remained in Bangkok, monitoring updates alongside countless others, hopeful that a resolution — or at least a functioning flight out — was close at hand.

The broader political crisis behind the airport siege remains unresolved, with protest leaders vowing to continue their occupation until their demands are met, leaving the fate of stranded travelers, and Thailand's battered tourism industry, hanging in the balance.

# Chaos Grips Bangkok as Airport Shutdown Strands Thousands

**BANGKOK** — Thailand's aviation network collapsed into chaos this week as anti-government protesters stormed and occupied the country's main airports, leaving tens of thousands of foreign tourists and business travelers stranded amid scenes of disorder that included reports of explosions and gunfire near demonstration sites.

Suvarnabhumi International Airport, one of Southeast Asia's busiest hubs, ground to a complete halt after members of the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD) breached security perimeters, set up encampments in terminals, and forced the cancellation of all incoming and outgoing flights. Don Mueang, the capital's secondary airport, was similarly overrun days later, compounding the crisis.

Passengers described scenes of confusion and fear. Long-haul travelers who had arrived expecting routine transfers instead found themselves sleeping on terminal floors, queuing for dwindling food supplies, and struggling for information as airline staff abandoned counters.

"We didn't know if we were safe or if we should try to leave," said one traveler, echoing accounts from stranded visitors who described sporadic bursts of gunfire and blasts audible near protest encampments outside the terminals, adding to the sense of a nation teetering on the edge of wider unrest. Thai authorities have not provided a definitive account of casualties or the origins of the violence, though local reports pointed to clashes between rival factions near the airport perimeter.

Foreign governments scrambled to respond. Embassies issued urgent travel advisories, and several countries began organizing alternative transport — including buses to airports in neighboring nations — to evacuate their citizens. Airlines rerouted flights to Phuket, Chiang Mai, and airports in Malaysia and Singapore, though capacity constraints left many travelers waiting days for a seat out of the country.

The airport seizures marked an escalation in months of political turmoil pitting the PAD against the government, part of a broader standoff over power, legitimacy, and the direction of Thai democracy. Business leaders warned of severe damage to the tourism industry, a pillar of the Thai economy, while diplomats cautioned that the unrest risked tarnishing the kingdom's reputation as a stable travel destination.

As night fell over the darkened terminals, the fate of the stranded — and of Thailand's political crisis — remained deeply uncertain.

*This is a developing story.*

---

*Note: This piece reflects the general contours of the 2008 Bangkok airport occupations. # Thai Protesters Shut Down Bangkok Airports, Stranding Thousands of Tourists

**BANGKOK** — Thousands of anti-government protesters from the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD) stormed and occupied Bangkok's two major airports this week, paralyzing air travel across Thailand and leaving an estimated 300,000 travelers stranded during one of the busiest tourist seasons of the year.

## Airports Overrun

Suvarnabhumi International Airport, Thailand's main international gateway, was forced to suspend all operations after yellow-shirted PAD demonstrators breached security barriers, set up encampments in terminals, and blocked runways with vehicles and makeshift barricades. Don Mueang Airport, which handles domestic and budget carrier flights, was similarly overrun days later as protesters expanded their occupation.

The PAD, which has accused the government of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat of being a proxy for ousted leader Thaksin Shinawatra, said the airport seizures were intended to force the administration's resignation. Protesters carried Thai flags, blew whistles, and chanted slogans while occupying check-in counters, departure lounges, and even the airport's control areas.

## Chaos for Travelers

Passengers described scenes of confusion and mounting frustration as flight boards flickered with cancellation notices and airline staff struggled to manage the crowds.

"We arrived at Suvarnabhumi at six in the morning for our flight home to Sydney, and the whole terminal was full of protesters wearing yellow shirts, blowing whistles like it was a football match," said Karen Doyle, an Australian tourist stranded with her husband for four days. "Nobody could tell us anything. The airline staff looked just as lost as we were."

Backpacker Miguel Fernandez, traveling from Spain, said he had been sleeping on the airport floor alongside hundreds of other travelers. "There's not enough food, not enough information. People are running out of medication. I saw a woman in tears because she couldn't reach her children back home to tell them she was safe," he said.

Some tourists reported being moved by Thai authorities to alternative accommodations or bused to airports in nearby provinces such as U-Tapao, Chiang Mai, and Krabi, which were pressed into service to handle emergency flights, though capacity remained limited.

"We were told to go to U-Tapao, three hours away by bus, just to get a flight out," said British tourist James Whitfield. "The bus itself took forever because of checkpoints and traffic. It felt like the whole country's transport system had collapsed."

## Airlines Scramble

Major carriers including Thai Airways, Qantas, British Airways, and Emirates canceled or diverted dozens of flights. Thai Airways alone reported grounding more than 200 flights, both domestic and international, with losses mounting into the tens of millions of dollars.

Airline representatives at makeshift help desks set up in hotel lobbies across Bangkok attempted to rebook passengers, but many said the process was slow and chaotic given the scale of the disruption.

"We've never seen anything like this," said one airline ground staff employee, who asked not to be named. "Normally we deal with weather delays or technical issues. This time, the airport itself is the problem."

## Government and Business Reaction

The Thai government condemned the airport takeover as illegal and appealed to the protesters to withdraw, warning of severe damage to the country's tourism industry and international reputation. Thailand's tourism sector, a major pillar of the economy, was already grappling with the global financial downturn, and industry groups warned that the airport siege could cost billions of dollars in lost revenue and further damage confidence in the country as a travel destination.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand issued advisories urging travelers to postpone nonessential trips, while several countries issued similar travel warnings for their citizens.

## Uncertain Resolution

As of this report, protesters showed no signs of ending their occupation, with PAD leaders vowing to continue until the government stepped down. Thai military and police officials have thus far avoided direct confrontation, wary of provoking violence, though tensions in and around the airport perimeter remain high.

For thousands of tourists like Doyle and Fernandez, the political standoff has turned dream vacations into extended, uncertain ordeals. "We just want to go home," Doyle said. "This isn't our fight, but we're the ones stuck in the middle of it."
